title: The Key That Turns Halfway
paragraphs: Table sugar dissolved in water can sit for years with little change, because the bond joining its two halves breaks far too slowly to notice.
A pinch of yeast begins splitting that bond at once, using a protein called invertase, one of thousands of enzymes that make slow chemistry fast.

Every enzyme raises two questions that are easy to confuse: how it recognizes one molecule among thousands drifting past, and how it then makes a reaction run millions of times faster than it otherwise would.
Both questions turn on the active site, a small cleft on the enzyme's surface where the reacting molecule, called the substrate, binds and is transformed.

In 1894 the German chemist Emil Fischer, working in Berlin, was studying enzymes that split glycosides, compounds in which glucose is joined to a partner by a bond that can point one of two ways, called alpha and beta.
A crude preparation from yeast split the alpha form and left the beta form untouched, while a preparation from almonds did exactly the reverse.
Fischer concluded that enzyme and substrate must fit together like a lock and a key: a key cut for the wrong lock, however similar, will not turn.

The proposal is remarkable for how little he had to go on: no one would show that an enzyme is a protein until James Sumner crystallized urease in 1926, so Fischer was describing the shape of something no one had seen.
The lock and key picture explained selectivity well, and it still does.
But a rigid lock has an awkward consequence: any smaller key should slip into the keyhole, and the smallest molecule in the cell is water, which fits nearly any pocket.
Consider hexokinase, the enzyme that begins the breakdown of glucose by moving a phosphate group from ATP onto the sugar.
Water carries the same reactive hydroxyl group as glucose, is far smaller, and is thousands of times more abundant, so a rigid lock would let the enzyme hand its phosphate to water almost constantly.
It does not: hexokinase transfers phosphate to water at a tiny fraction of the rate at which it transfers phosphate to glucose.
Something about glucose, beyond merely fitting, switches the enzyme on.
In 1958 the American biochemist Daniel Koshland, then at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York, proposed the answer he called induced fit.
An enzyme, in his view, is less a lock than a glove: the hand goes in, and the glove changes shape to meet it.
The substrate's arrival pulls the enzyme into a new shape that brings the catalytic groups of the active site into working position, and only a substrate able to cause that shift gets a reaction.
A molecule that fits the pocket but cannot move the protein may bind and simply sit there; water is ignored not because it fails to fit but because it is too small to move anything.
Koshland had inferred all this indirectly; it took twenty years to see it.
In 1978 Thomas Steitz and his colleagues at Yale University compared X-ray structures of yeast hexokinase with and without glucose bound.
The empty enzyme has two lobes with a deep cleft between them, and the sugar settles at the bottom of the cleft.
Once it is there, the two lobes swing together and close over it, so that the glucose is nearly buried and the water that had filled the cleft is squeezed out.
The closing brings the catalytic machinery to bear on the sugar's sixth carbon, where the phosphate will attach, and removes the water that might otherwise have accepted it.
Textbooks like to set the two models against each other, as though Koshland had overthrown Fischer, and I think that framing does both men a disservice.
Fischer's claim that recognition depends on complementary shape has never been in doubt; what Koshland added was that the complementary shape need not exist until the substrate helps create it.
Many enzymes barely move when their substrates bind, and for them the old key still turns the old lock.
The deeper limitation of both models is that they concern recognition, and recognition by itself does not make a reaction faster.

Picture a reaction as a journey over a hill: reactants rest in one valley and products in another, and between them the atoms must pass through a strained, fleeting arrangement, old bonds half broken and new ones half formed, that chemists call the transition state.
The height of the hill above the starting valley is the activation energy, a term that goes back to the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius in the 1880s.
Only molecules with enough energy to reach the top can cross, and because their number falls off steeply as the hill grows higher, even a modest reduction in its height greatly increases the rate.
Lowering the hill is the whole business of catalysis, and the question becomes how an enzyme manages it.
The answer was sketched in 1946 by Linus Pauling, who noticed a flaw in the idea of a perfect fit.
An enzyme shaped exactly to match its substrate would bind it and then hold it, since every contact would reward the substrate for staying as it is.
Pauling argued instead that the active site is complementary not to the substrate but to the transition state.
It grips the substrate loosely and the awkward halfway arrangement tightly, so that part of the climb is paid for by contacts the enzyme makes along the way.
On this account the perfect lock would be the worst possible catalyst; an enzyme succeeds because its key does not fit well until it is halfway through turning.
Pauling's proposal carried a prediction: a stable molecule shaped like the transition state should bind an enzyme far more tightly than the substrate does.
Such molecules, called transition-state analogs, do exist, and many bind thousands or even millions of times more tightly than the real substrate.

The most striking test came in 1986, when groups led by Richard Lerner in La Jolla, California, and Peter Schultz in Berkeley independently raised antibodies against a mimic of the transition state of an ester bond being split by water.
The antibodies, which have no history as catalysts, split the ester.

I find the result elegant and its limits instructive: the antibodies worked far more slowly than natural enzymes, so a snug fit to the transition state is clearly part of what an enzyme does and just as clearly not all of it.

In 1995 Richard Wolfenden and Anna Radzicka at the University of North Carolina measured how fast a step in nucleotide synthesis, the loss of carbon dioxide from a molecule called orotidine monophosphate, proceeds in water with no enzyme present.
They had to heat sealed samples and extrapolate downward, because at room temperature the reaction has a half-life of about 78 million years.
The enzyme that performs the step in cells finishes it in a few hundredths of a second.
The speeding factor is roughly a hundred million billion, among the largest ever measured, achieved without heat, pressure, or harsh chemicals.
One thing an enzyme cannot do deserves equal emphasis, because students, and occasionally textbooks, get it wrong: an enzyme does not change where a reaction ends up.

The ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium is fixed by the energy difference between the two valleys, and the enzyme, unchanged when the reaction is over, leaves that difference as it found it.
What it lowers is the hill between the valleys, and a lower hill is lower from both sides, so the reverse reaction is accelerated by precisely the same factor as the forward one.
A tunnel bored through a mountain shortens the trip without moving either town, and traffic uses it in both directions.
The enzyme's gift is time: it brings the cell to a destination chemistry had already chosen, within the lifetime of a cell rather than of a mountain range.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the active site of an enzyme is
choices: the bond in a sugar molecule that breaks too slowly to notice
a protein in yeast that splits table sugar into its two halves
a small cleft on the enzyme's surface where the substrate binds
the part of the substrate that the enzyme recognizes by its shape
the strained, fleeting arrangement of atoms at the top of the energy hill

proof.quote: a small cleft on the enzyme's surface where the reacting molecule, called the substrate, binds

questions.why: Paragraph 1 defines the active site directly: a small cleft on the enzyme's surface where the reacting molecule, called the substrate, binds and is transformed.
distractorNotes: Wrong object: the slow-breaking bond in paragraph 1 belongs to table sugar, not to the enzyme.
Wrong object: that describes invertase, the enzyme itself, not a site on it.
Reversed: the active site is on the enzyme, and the substrate is the molecule that binds to it.
Wrong paragraph: that is the transition state, defined in paragraph 7.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Fischer's preparation from yeast
choices: split both the alpha and the beta forms of the glycoside
split the beta form of the glycoside but not the alpha form
split neither form until a preparation from almonds was added
was shown to be a protein when it was crystallized in 1926
split the alpha form of the glycoside but not the beta form

proof.quote: A crude preparation from yeast split the alpha form and left the beta form untouched

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says the crude preparation from yeast split the alpha form and left the beta form untouched, while the almond preparation did the reverse.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 2 says the yeast preparation left the beta form untouched.
Reversed: that is what the almond preparation did, not the yeast preparation.
Outside the passage: nothing says the two preparations were ever combined.
Wrong enzyme: the protein crystallized in 1926 was urease, by James Sumner.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that when Fischer proposed the lock and key model, he
choices: could not have known the chemical nature of the enzymes he studied
had already seen the three-dimensional shape of an enzyme's active site
based the model on crystals of urease that he had prepared himself
believed that the enzymes from yeast and from almonds were the same
relied on the X-ray structures that were available to him at the time

proof.quote: no one would show that an enzyme is a protein until James Sumner crystallized urease in 1926, so Fischer was describing the shape of something no one had seen

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says no one would show that an enzyme is a protein until 1926, thirty years after Fischer's proposal, and that he was describing the shape of something no one had seen. So in 1894 he could not have known what enzymes were made of.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 2 says Fischer was describing the shape of something no one had seen.
Wrong person: it was James Sumner who crystallized urease, and not until 1926.
Contradicted: the two preparations behaved in opposite ways, which is the whole point of the experiment.
Anachronism: the first X-ray structures the passage mentions date from 1978.

questions.stem: The author discusses water in paragraph 3 primarily to
choices: explain how hexokinase begins the breakdown of glucose inside the cell
show that water is the most abundant molecule in a living cell
argue that the lock and key model fails to explain selectivity
expose a prediction of the rigid lock that the enzyme does not obey
introduce the two lobes that close around glucose in hexokinase

proof.quote: so a rigid lock would let the enzyme hand its phosphate to water almost constantly
It does not

questions.why: Paragraph 3 sets up what a rigid lock would predict, that the enzyme would hand its phosphate to water almost constantly, and then says flatly that it does not. Water is there to show the prediction failing.
distractorNotes: Too narrow: hexokinase is described only as a vehicle for the water problem, not for its own sake.
Wrong purpose: the passage mentions water's abundance to sharpen the prediction, not to rank molecules in the cell.
Contradicted: paragraph 3 opens by saying the model explained selectivity well, and still does.
Wrong paragraph: the closing lobes do not appear until paragraph 5.

questions.stem: According to Koshland's model as the passage describes it, a molecule receives a reaction from an enzyme only if it
choices: is smaller than the pocket of the active site and fits inside it loosely
pulls the enzyme into a shape that puts its catalytic groups in place
binds the active site more tightly than the transition state does
is present at a concentration thousands of times higher than water
matches the active site exactly, the way a key matches a rigid lock

proof.quote: only a substrate able to cause that shift gets a reaction

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the substrate's arrival pulls the enzyme into a new shape that brings the catalytic groups into working position, and only a substrate able to cause that shift gets a reaction.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 4 says a molecule that fits but cannot move the protein may bind and simply sit there.
Wrong paragraph: tight binding of the transition state is Pauling's idea in paragraph 8.
Reversed and irrelevant: water is the abundant one, and abundance earns it nothing.
Wrong model: an exact match to a rigid lock is Fischer's picture, the one Koshland revised.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 1978 structures of yeast hexokinase showed that when glucose binds,
choices: the sugar remains loosely held at the mouth of the cleft between the two lobes
water is drawn into the cleft so that it can accept the phosphate
the enzyme's two lobes separate to expose the sugar's sixth carbon atom
the phosphate group is transferred from the sugar back onto ATP
the two lobes close over the sugar and squeeze water out of the cleft

proof.quote: the two lobes swing together and close over it, so that the glucose is nearly buried and the water that had filled the cleft is squeezed out

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says that once the sugar settles at the bottom of the cleft, the two lobes swing together and close over it, burying the glucose and squeezing out the water that had filled the cleft.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: the sugar settles at the bottom of the cleft and is nearly buried, not held loosely at the mouth.
Reversed: water is squeezed out of the cleft precisely so it cannot accept the phosphate.
Reversed: the lobes close rather than separate.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the phosphate moves from ATP onto the sugar.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage about hexokinase EXCEPT:
choices: Without the enzyme its reaction takes about 78 million years.
It moves a phosphate group from ATP onto glucose.
Its empty form has two lobes with a deep cleft between them.
It transfers phosphate to water far more slowly than to glucose.
Its structure was examined by X-ray methods at Yale University.

proof.quote: moving a phosphate group from ATP onto the sugar
The empty enzyme has two lobes with a deep cleft between them
hexokinase transfers phosphate to water at a tiny fraction of the rate at which it transfers phosphate to glucose
Thomas Steitz and his colleagues at Yale University compared X-ray structures of yeast hexokinase
the reaction has a half-life of about 78 million years

questions.why: The 78 million year half-life in paragraph 10 belongs to the orotidine monophosphate reaction studied by Wolfenden and Radzicka, not to hexokinase. The other four statements are all in paragraphs 3 and 5.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 3: hexokinase begins the breakdown of glucose by moving a phosphate group from ATP onto the sugar.
Stated in paragraph 5: the empty enzyme has two lobes with a deep cleft between them.
Stated in paragraph 3: it transfers phosphate to water at a tiny fraction of the rate for glucose.
Stated in paragraph 5: Steitz and colleagues at Yale compared its X-ray structures.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward textbooks that present lock and key and induced fit as rival models is best described as
choices: amused
critical
indifferent
admiring
bewildered

proof.quote: I think that framing does both men a disservice

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says plainly that the textbook framing does both men a disservice, and then explains what each man actually contributed. That is a critic correcting a habit, not a reader enjoying it or puzzled by it.
distractorNotes: Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 6 treats the framing as funny.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position and argues for it.
Reversed: the author objects to the framing rather than praising it.
Wrong register: the author explains the problem confidently, not in confusion.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, the word 'modest' most nearly means
choices: humble about one's own achievements
reluctant to draw attention to oneself
small in size or amount
unpretentious or simple in style
decent and proper in behavior

proof.quote: even a modest reduction in its height greatly increases the rate

questions.why: Paragraph 7 contrasts a modest reduction in the hill's height with a large increase in rate, so the word is sizing the reduction: a small one. The everyday sense of being humble has nothing to do with a hill.
distractorNotes: This is the common meaning of the word, but a reduction in height cannot be humble.
Same problem: the sentence is about the size of a change, not anyone's personality.
Style is not at issue; the sentence is comparing a small cause with a large effect.
Another everyday sense of the word, and it cannot apply to the height of a hill.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Pauling argued that an enzyme's active site is complementary to
choices: the substrate in its resting, unstrained form
the products that rest in the second valley
any molecule small enough to fit the pocket
the transition state rather than the substrate
a stable analog that mimics the transition state

proof.quote: the active site is complementary not to the substrate but to the transition state

questions.why: Paragraph 8 states Pauling's argument in one line: the active site is complementary not to the substrate but to the transition state.
distractorNotes: Reversed: a site matched to the resting substrate is exactly the perfect fit Pauling faulted, one that would hold the substrate as it is.
Outside the passage: Pauling's argument says nothing about matching the products.
Wrong paragraph: the small-key problem belongs to the rigid lock in paragraph 3.
Half right: analogs appear in paragraph 9 as a later test of the idea, not as what Pauling said the site matches.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an enzyme makes its tightest contacts with a reacting molecule when that molecule
choices: has just settled into the active site in its original form
has been fully converted into the product and is about to leave the site
is present at a concentration many thousands of times higher than usual
is held in the enzyme's pocket without having triggered any shift
is midway through the change, its bonds half broken and half formed

proof.quote: It grips the substrate loosely and the awkward halfway arrangement tightly
old bonds half broken and new ones half formed, that chemists call the transition state

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the enzyme grips the substrate loosely and the awkward halfway arrangement tightly, and paragraph 7 defines that halfway arrangement as the transition state, with old bonds half broken and new ones half formed. Put the two lines together and the tightest grip comes midway through the change.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the substrate in its original form is gripped loosely.
Outside the passage: nothing describes the enzyme's grip on the finished product.
Unrelated: concentration appears in paragraph 3 about water, not about the tightness of binding.
Wrong paragraph: a molecule that binds without triggering a shift simply sits there, in Koshland's account.

questions.stem: The author mentions the catalytic antibodies of 1986 in paragraph 9 primarily to
choices: present a test of Pauling's idea and mark the limit of what it shows
argue that antibodies will eventually replace natural enzymes in industry
show that transition-state analogs bind more tightly than substrates
demonstrate that Koshland's induced fit also applies to antibodies
prove that a snug fit to the transition state fully explains enzyme speed

proof.quote: The most striking test came in 1986
clearly part of what an enzyme does and just as clearly not all of it

questions.why: Paragraph 9 calls the antibodies the most striking test of Pauling's prediction, then uses their slowness to say that fit to the transition state is clearly part of what an enzyme does and just as clearly not all of it. The example is there to confirm the idea and to bound it.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing is said about industry or about replacing enzymes.
Wrong sentence: that is the point of the transition-state analogs earlier in paragraph 9, not of the antibodies.
Outside the passage: Koshland's model is never connected to antibodies.
Reversed: the author says the fit is not all of it, because the antibodies worked far more slowly than natural enzymes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Wolfenden and Radzicka determined the uncatalyzed rate of the orotidine monophosphate reaction by
choices: measuring the reaction directly over a period of 78 million years
raising antibodies against a mimic of its transition state
comparing X-ray structures with and without the enzyme bound
heating sealed samples and extrapolating to room temperature
timing the enzyme as it finished the step in a fraction of a second

proof.quote: They had to heat sealed samples and extrapolate downward

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says they had to heat sealed samples and extrapolate downward, because at room temperature the reaction has a half-life of about 78 million years.
distractorNotes: Impossible by the passage's own numbers: a 78 million year half-life is why they could not measure it directly.
Wrong paragraph: raising antibodies is the 1986 experiment in paragraph 9.
Wrong paragraph: X-ray structures belong to the hexokinase work in paragraph 5.
Wrong measurement: the question asks about the rate without the enzyme, not with it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of an enzyme EXCEPT:
choices: It is unchanged when the reaction is over.
It lowers the hill between the reactant and product valleys.
It shifts the equilibrium ratio of products to reactants.
It speeds the reverse reaction as much as the forward one.
It brings a reaction to its destination far sooner.

proof.quote: unchanged when the reaction is over
What it lowers is the hill between the valleys
the reverse reaction is accelerated by precisely the same factor as the forward one
within the lifetime of a cell rather than of a mountain range
an enzyme does not change where a reaction ends up

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says an enzyme does not change where a reaction ends up and leaves the energy difference between the valleys as it found it, so the equilibrium ratio is the one thing it cannot shift. The other four statements are all in paragraph 11.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 11: the enzyme is unchanged when the reaction is over.
Stated in paragraph 11: what it lowers is the hill between the valleys.
Stated in paragraph 11: the reverse reaction is accelerated by precisely the same factor as the forward one.
Stated in paragraph 11: it brings the cell to its destination within the lifetime of a cell rather than of a mountain range.

questions.stem: A chemist adds an enzyme to a flask in which its reaction has already reached equilibrium. Which outcome does the principle described in paragraph 11 predict?
choices: The amount of product rises, because the enzyme lowers the hill
The amounts of reactant and product remain where they were
The reaction runs backward, because the enzyme favors the lower valley
The amount of product falls as the enzyme is consumed
The amount of product rises slowly, then returns to its old value

proof.quote: an enzyme does not change where a reaction ends up
a lower hill is lower from both sides, so the reverse reaction is accelerated by precisely the same factor as the forward one
shortens the trip without moving either town

questions.why: Paragraph 11's rule is that an enzyme does not change where a reaction ends up: it speeds both directions by the same factor and moves neither town. A flask already at its endpoint has nowhere to go, so the amounts stay put.
distractorNotes: Reversed: lowering the hill speeds both directions equally, so it cannot push the mixture toward product.
Contradicted: the enzyme does not favor either valley; it leaves the energy difference as it found it.
Contradicted: paragraph 11 says the enzyme is unchanged when the reaction is over.
Contradicted: nothing in the rule allows even a temporary departure from the endpoint.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if an enzyme speeds a forward reaction by a factor of one million, the reverse reaction would be
choices: slowed by a factor of one million
unaffected, since the enzyme acts only in one direction
sped up, but by a smaller factor than the forward reaction
prevented entirely, since the product is removed as it forms
sped up by a factor of one million as well

proof.quote: the reverse reaction is accelerated by precisely the same factor as the forward one

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says a lower hill is lower from both sides, so the reverse reaction is accelerated by precisely the same factor as the forward one. Apply that to a factor of one million and the reverse gets the same million.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the reverse reaction is accelerated, not slowed.
Contradicted: the tunnel in paragraph 11 carries traffic in both directions.
Contradicted: the passage says precisely the same factor, not a smaller one.
Outside the passage: nothing in paragraph 11 says the product is removed.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Koshland's induced fit model replaced Fischer's lock and key model, which biochemists have since abandoned as mistaken
Hexokinase is the best understood of all enzymes because its closing lobes were seen directly in X-ray structures in 1978
The catalytic antibodies of 1986 prove that any protein shaped to fit a transition state will work as well as a natural enzyme
Enzymes recognize substrates by shape and speed reactions by binding the transition state, without moving the endpoint
Enzymes speed reactions chiefly by shifting the equilibrium toward products, and they emerge unchanged when the reaction ends

proof.quote: Every enzyme raises two questions that are easy to confuse
complementary not to the substrate but to the transition state
an enzyme does not change where a reaction ends up

questions.why: Paragraph 1 sets up two questions, recognition and speed; the middle paragraphs answer recognition with shape and speed with the transition state; paragraph 11 adds what an enzyme cannot do. Only one choice covers all three parts without overstating any of them.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 6 says Fischer's claim has never been in doubt and that the old key still turns for many enzymes.
Too narrow: hexokinase is one example, and the passage never ranks it against other enzymes.
Contradicted: paragraph 9 says the antibodies worked far more slowly than natural enzymes.
Contradicted: paragraph 11 says an enzyme does not shift the equilibrium at all.
